pumac-2022-finals-a-01.title: Classify all such f
pumac-2022-finals-a-01.body:
**Answer.** $f(x)=x+1999$ for all $x$ outside a set $F$ of fixed points (and $f(x)=x$ for $x\in F$), where $F\subseteq\mathbb Z_{>0}$ satisfies: $1\notin F$, and if $z\in F$ and $z>1999$ then $z-1999\in F$. In particular $f(x)=x+1999$ for all $x$ is the solution without fixed points. (Equivalently: on each residue class mod $1999$ the fixed points form an initial segment; the class of $1$ has none.)

**These work.** If $x\in F$, then $f^k(x)=x$. If $x\notin F$, then $x+1999j\notin F$ for all $j\ge0$ (otherwise descending by the closure property would put $x$ in $F$), so $f^k(x)=x+1999k$, and $k\mid1999k$. Also $f(x)-x\in\{0,1999\}$ and $f(1)=2000$.

**There are no others.**

1. *$f$ is injective.* If $f(x)=f(y)$ then $f^k(x)=f^k(y)$ for all $k\ge1$, and $k\mid f^k(x)-x$, $k\mid f^k(y)-y$ give $k\mid x-y$ for all $k$; so $x=y$.
2. *No cycles except fixed points.* Let $x_j=f^j(x)$. If $x_m=x_0$ with $m\ge2$ minimal, take $k=tm+1$: $x_k=x_1$, so $(tm+1)\mid x_1-x_0\ne0$ for every $t$, impossible. By injectivity, a point that is not fixed therefore has pairwise distinct iterates $x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots$.
3. *Behaviour of a non-fixed orbit.* Write $x_k=x_0+kq_k$ (as $k\mid x_k-x_0$). For $k\ge x_0$ positivity forces $q_k\ge0$, and $q_k\ne0$ since $x_k\ne x_0$, so $q_k\ge1$. From $x_{k+1}-x_k\le2023$ we get $(k+1)q_{k+1}\le kq_k+2023$. If $k\ge2023$ and $q_{k+1}\ge q_k+1$, then $(k+1)(q_k+1)\le kq_k+2023$ would give $q_k+k+1\le2023$, false. So $q_k$ is eventually non-increasing, hence eventually a constant $q\ge1$, and then $x_{k+1}-x_k=(k+1)q-kq=q$ for large $k$.
   Put $d_j=x_{j+1}-x_j$. Since $k\mid x_k-x_0$ and $k\mid x_{k+1}-x_1$, we get $k\mid d_k-d_0$ for all $k$. For large $k$, $d_k=q$, so $k\mid q-d_0$ for all large $k$, forcing $d_0=q$. The same applies to every $x_j$ (same tail, same $q$), so $d_j=q$ for all $j$: the orbit of $x$ is $x,x+q,x+2q,\dots$ with $1\le q\le2023$.
4. *The step is $1999$.* The orbit of $1$ is $1,2000,3999,\dots=\{1+1999i\}$. Let $x\ne$ fixed have step $q$. If the two progressions share a value $f^i(1)=f^j(x)$ with $i,j$ minimal, injectivity forces $i=0$ or $j=0$; $i=0$ is impossible ($f^j(x)>1$ unless $x=1$), and $j=0$ means $x=1+1999i$, so $q=1999$. Otherwise the progressions are disjoint. But $1999$ is prime, so if $1999\nmid q$ the progressions $1+1999i$ and $x+qj$ do meet (Chinese Remainder Theorem, with large $i,j\ge0$). Hence $1999\mid q$, and $q\le2023$ gives $q=1999$.
   So $f(x)=x+1999$ for every non-fixed $x$.
5. *Conditions on $F$.* $1\notin F$ because $f(1)=2000$. If $z\in F$, $z>1999$ and $z-1999\notin F$, then $f(z-1999)=z=f(z)$ contradicts injectivity. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2022-finals-a-03.title: Remove the largest entry
pumac-2022-finals-a-03.body:
**Answer: $F_{n+3}-2$**, where $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{k+2}=F_{k+1}+F_k$. For $n=1,2,3,\dots$ this is $1,3,6,11,19,32,\dots$

**Construction.** Use the numbers $F_2,F_3,\dots,F_{n+1}$ once each, arranged around the circle as: $F_2=1$, then the odd-indexed ones $F_3,F_5,F_7,\dots$ in increasing order, then the even-indexed ones in decreasing order $\dots,F_6,F_4$, and back to $F_2$. For $n=6$ this is $(1,2,5,13,8,3)$; for $n=5$, $(1,2,5,8,3)$; for $n=3$, $(1,2,3)$.

It is nice: $\gcd=1$ because of the entry $1$. Along either monotone run, a middle element $F_k$ has neighbours $F_{k-2},F_{k+2}$ with $F_{k-2}+F_{k+2}=3F_k$ (at the ends, $F_1=F_2=1$ plays the role of $F_{k-2}$ next to $F_3$ and $F_4$). At the turning point the largest element $F_{n+1}$ sits between $F_n$ and $F_{n-1}$, whose sum is $F_{n+1}$. The neighbour $F_n$ has its other neighbour $F_{n-2}$ and $F_{n+1}+F_{n-2}=F_n+F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}=2F_n$; the neighbour $F_{n-1}$ has its other neighbour $F_{n-3}$ and $F_{n+1}+F_{n-3}=2F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}+F_{n-3}=3F_{n-1}$. The sum of the entries is $F_2+\dots+F_{n+1}=F_{n+3}-2$.

**Upper bound.** For a nice $m$-tuple $T$ consider the statements

- (i) every entry is $\le F_{m+1}$;
- (ii) the sum of any two cyclically adjacent entries is $\le F_{m+2}$;
- (iii) the total is $\le F_{m+3}-2$.

*Base cases.* $m=1$: $T=(1)$. $m=2$: $a_1\mid2a_2$, $a_2\mid2a_1$, $\gcd=1$ give $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$. In both cases (i)-(iii) hold ($F_2=1,F_3=2,F_4=3,F_5=5$).

*Adjacent entries are coprime for $m\ge3$:* if a prime $p$ divides $a_i$ and $a_{i+1}$, then $a_i\mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$ gives $p\mid a_{i-1}$ and $a_{i+1}\mid a_i+a_{i+2}$ gives $p\mid a_{i+2}$; continuing in both directions, $p$ divides every entry, contradicting $\gcd=1$.

*Induction step, $m\ge3$.* Let $M$ be a largest entry with neighbours $x,y$ (distinct positions). Then $M\mid x+y\le2M$, so $x+y=M$ or $x+y=2M$.

- If $x+y=2M$ then $x=y=M$ are adjacent to $M$, so $M=1$ by coprimality and $T$ consists of $1$'s; then (i)-(iii) clearly hold (the total $m\le F_{m+3}-2$).
- If $x+y=M$, delete $M$ to get an $(m-1)$-tuple $T'$ in which $x,y$ are adjacent. It is nice: for the neighbour $z$ of $x$ on the other side, $x\mid z+M=z+x+y$ gives $x\mid z+y$, and similarly for $y$; all other conditions are unchanged; and if a number divides all entries of $T'$ it divides $x+y=M$, so $\gcd=1$.

Now use the hypothesis for $T'$ (length $m-1$): (ii) gives $M=x+y\le F_{m+1}$, hence (i) for $T$. Every entry of $T'$ is $\le F_m$ by (i), so the adjacent sums involving $M$ are $M+x,\,M+y\le F_{m+1}+F_m=F_{m+2}$, and adjacent sums not involving $M$ are adjacent in $T'$, so $\le F_{m+1}$: this is (ii) for $T$. Finally by (iii) for $T'$,
$$\text{sum}(T)=\text{sum}(T')+M\le(F_{m+2}-2)+F_{m+1}=F_{m+3}-2 .$$
So (i)-(iii) hold for all $m$, and the maximum is $F_{n+3}-2$. $\blacksquare$

(A brute-force search for $n\le6$ gives $1,3,6,11,19,32$.)
